extracted.intended_audience: NLP and multimodal-model researchers working on patent analysis and generation
extracted.subtask_description: A broad survey of natural language processing and multimodal techniques applied to patent documents, covering patent fundamentals, structural/linguistic characteristics, datasets, task definitions, methods, and evaluation metrics for analysis and generation tasks. Intended to orient researchers to challenges and opportunities in patent NLP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable a technical solution must be (1) new (novelty), (2) involve an inventive step (non-obviousness), and (3) be industrially applicable (utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive examination compares the invention with earlier prior art from patent literature or any public source. The utility requirement may be applied less strictly in many offices; examination also enforces formal and procedural requirements. Novelty/inventiveness are core to novelty prediction tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent document structure and required sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent documents normally include publication information, title, bibliometric information, patent classification, citations, abstract, background, detailed description, claims, and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For dataset curation and automated processing, segmenting documents into these sections (abstract, claims, description, etc.) is a recommended preprocessing step. Each section serves different analytical/generative roles (e.g., descriptions contain details; claims define legal scope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims drafting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the legal scope of the patent; each claim is a single sentence describing specific features that make the invention novel and non-obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be carefully and precisely crafted to define boundaries that can withstand legal scrutiny. Claim wording must be consistent with descriptions and reference numbers; small wording differences can dramatically change scope. Automated claim generation must prioritize precision and legal defensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Each technical term must be used consistently throughout the document; self-defined or coined terms are common in patents and must not be replaced by other words unless equivalence is explicitly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High repetitiveness and strict term consistency are expected; models and preprocessing should preserve and respect defined term usage. Paraphrasing for readability is an anti-pattern in patent drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference numbers and figure-term consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference numbers in drawings must be named by the same term consistently throughout the patent application, even when deviating from normal language conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated extraction and generation systems must track and maintain consistent mappings between reference numbers and terms across text and figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed description completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The detailed description must provide comprehensive details about the invention and specific embodiments, typically discussing the drawings to support the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent analysis and generation should prioritize full descriptions (not just titles or abstracts) because they contain essential technical details; training/evaluation datasets should include description sections when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-context handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent descriptions are very long (average patent description tokens can exceed 11,000), which exceeds many LLMs' default context windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models for patent tasks should support long context (e.g., long-range attention, extended window LLMs) or use segmentation/summarization strategies. Failure to handle long context is a critical challenge for accurate analysis/generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific terminology and technical language
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent language is highly technical and often contains newly coined or law-specific terms that differ from general-domain corpora.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domain adaptation or patent-specific pretraining improves performance; general LLMs trained on colloquial corpora may fail to capture defined terms or their patent-specific senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision requirement of patent text
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent texts prioritize precision and information density over readability; sentences often include multiple clauses and strict definitions to ensure enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generation models must minimize small lexical variations that alter legal meaning. High repetitiveness and constrained paraphrase are normal; evaluation must check for precision, not just fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-processing and dataset curation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-processing steps should segment patent documents into defined sections and rectify irregularities like missing fields, erroneous characters, and formatting issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because patent offices rarely provide pre-processed structured datasets, researchers should perform careful cleaning and section segmentation to improve downstream model performance. Document-level normalization and error correction are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal integration guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents can include drawings and metadata; multimodal methods that combine text, images, and quantitative metadata may yield more comprehensive results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text is the primary legally binding carrier (claims/descriptions), so multimodal approaches should treat images as complementary. Many drawings are generic/low quality, so models must handle noisy visual inputs; hybrid (text+image+metadata) methods are recommended where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metadata (citations, classifications, actors) in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Metadata such as citations, classification codes, inventors, applicants, assignees, and examiners provide high-level relational information useful for retrieval, classification, and valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating citation graphs and metadata embeddings can improve performance (e.g., ~6% improvement reported). But classification codes may be coarse and misleading; rely on metadata as a complement to textual analysis, not a substitute for full description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated subject classification task definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated subject classification is a multi-label classification task: given patent content (title, abstract, claims), predict one or multiple IPC/CPC class labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation methods include top-1 prediction, top-N guesses, and all-categories matching. Multiple methodological approaches exist: feature-based classifiers, fine-tuned transformers, and hybrid methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent classification schemes (IPC/CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: International Patent Classification (IPC) and Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) are hierarchical schemes (sections, classes, subclasses, main groups, sub-groups) used to categorize patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifier outputs should map to these hierarchical codes; system design may leverage hierarchy for multi-label prediction and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification evaluation methods (top-1, top-N, all-categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three evaluation approaches: top prediction checks if top-1 equals main class; top-N succeeds if any of top-N matches main class; all-categories checks whether top-1 is in the set of main and incidental classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top-N is more flexible; choice depends on downstream use (e.g., examiner assistance vs exact labelling). Reporting multiple of these measures is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification metrics and averaging (accuracy, precision, recall, F1; macro vs micro)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1. For multi-class/multi-label tasks use macro-averaging (equal weight per class) or micro-averaging (aggregate counts across classes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Micro-averaging is preferred by default for class-imbalanced data because it weights frequent classes more appropriately. Report both when possible to capture per-class and overall performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent information retrieval task and metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent retrieval aims to retrieve target patent documents from databases; standard IR metrics include precision, recall, mean average precision (MAP), and patent-specific PRES.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRES evaluates ranking deviation of relevant documents; retrieval can leverage metadata, citation graphs, text embeddings, and image features. Choose metrics aligned with user needs (recall-important prior-art search vs precision-oriented tasks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent retrieval: metadata- and image-based method considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Metadata (citations, classes, inventors) can improve retrieval; image-based retrieval is possible but has historically lower performance due to generic or low-resolution drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybrid representations (text + metadata + images) often outperform single-modality approaches; image-specific architectures and large curated datasets (e.g., DeepPatent) improve image retrieval performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information extraction from patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Information extraction focuses on extracting desired structured information (entities, relationships, claims, figures) from patent texts for downstream tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IE systems must account for idiosyncratic patent phrasing, self-defined terms, and noisy figures/metadata; high-quality labeled data is limited for some IE sub-tasks, requiring task-specific dataset creation or silver-standard labeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assessment tasks (novelty, granting, litigation, valuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality assessment includes predicting novelty, whether an application will be granted, litigation likelihood, and patent valuation as proxies for patent quality and scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tasks incorporate textual signals and metadata; e.g., unclear or ambiguous claims and scarce descriptions increase litigation risk. Granting prediction must consider formal/legal language and document completeness beyond novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty proxy and dataset caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets sometimes proxy novelty using indirect signals (e.g., patents connected to major awards considered novel; patents granted by USPTO but rejected by EPO and JPO considered lacking novelty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: such proxies may deviate from formal novelty definitions used in examination and can introduce bias into novelty-prediction models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation risk indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents with unclear or ambiguous claims or very scarce descriptions tend to have higher likelihoods of being subject to litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigation-prediction models should include measures of claim clarity, description completeness, and possibly citation/network features to improve predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent valuation as reflection of quality and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent valuation aims to measure the economic or strategic value of patents, reflecting patent quality and breadth of protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuation models combine textual features, citations, classifications, and market/company metadata; valuation is multi-faceted and task-specific evaluation criteria should be defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology forecasting and innovation recommendation tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use patent corpora to predict future technology trends (forecasting) and to recommend novel combinations or ideas (innovation recommendation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks leverage longitudinal patent data, classification trajectories, citation networks, and embeddings; evaluation criteria depend on forecasting horizons and recommendation utility metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared task / benchmark importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared tasks (e.g., CLEF-IP, NTCIR, TREC-CHEM) provide curated datasets and common tasks to enable fair comparison among methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participating in shared tasks or using their datasets is recommended to allow reproducible, comparable evaluation; benchmarks often include text, images, and metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure caption and formal minimal wording requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Figure captions in many patents often contain minimal wording to satisfy formalities (e.g., 'Figure n depicts another embodiment of the invention'), as required by formal regulations (European Patent Regulations Rule 42(d), PCT Rule 5.1(a)(iv), US 37 CFR 1.74).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caption-generation systems must recognize that many captions are intentionally terse; generating legally problematic or overly detailed captions might conflict with disclosure strategy. Datasets may contain both brief and detailed captions (e.g., PatentDesc, IMPACT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Image/drawing limitations for automated processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drawings are often generic, schematic, low-resolution, or lack accompanying descriptive text, which limits their usefulness for automated processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Image-only classification/retrieval performs worse than text-based approaches in many cases; use images as complementary inputs and apply specialized encoders for patent figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics for text generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Text generation evaluation includes human evaluation (gold standard) and automated metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, and BERTScore; automated metrics compare generated text against reference texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human evaluation is reliable but costly; BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR have limitations (focus on n-gram overlap), while BERTScore captures semantic similarity. Use multiple metrics and human assessment for patent generation tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keystroke-based evaluation for generative patent tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Keystroke-based evaluation measures the number of keystrokes saved by model autocomplete suggestions (a productivity metric for claim drafting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported results are task- and model-dependent; this metric may not correlate with legal correctness or claim quality. Use alongside other quality/human-evaluation metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: PatentEval human-evaluation framework
rubrics_metrics.description: PatentEval categorizes machine-generated patent text errors into types such as grammatical errors, irrelevant content, incomplete coverage, and clarity issues for structured human evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying PatentEval provides targeted feedback on common LLM failures in patent drafting and can guide model improvements; use for systematic human evaluation of generative outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold vs silver-standard datasets and labeling trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some patent tasks (e.g., simplification) lack gold-standard labels due to cost/expertise constraints; silver-standard data generated by automated tools is sometimes used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limitations of silver standards (noise, bias). When possible, create expert-labeled gold data for critical evaluation or use silver labels with caution and validation subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation and ranking-specific metrics (MAP, PRES) for retrieval
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean average precision (MAP) and patent retrieval evaluation score (PRES) quantify retrieval ranking quality; PRES measures average deviation of relevant documents' ranks from ideal ordering, normalized by maximum returned documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MAP for standard IR ranking comparisons; use PRES when evaluating patent-specific prior-art search systems and ranking quality with respect to relevance positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and benchmarking practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Because tasks and datasets vary widely, researchers should report dataset preprocessing steps, exact sections used (abstract/claims/description), evaluation metrics, and averaging methods to enable reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared tasks and large curated datasets (e.g., HUPD) are recommended to standardize comparisons. Explicitly document proxies used for labels (e.g., novelty proxies) and limitations.
